body:
Monthly SEO report template for clients: what to include and what to leave out. A well-built monthly SEO report shows the client exactly what happened that month, without forcing them to decipher raw exports from Search Console or Analytics themselves.

Many agencies send long reports full of charts that clients never get around to reading. A good report answers within two minutes whether the month was worth the investment.

Monthly SEO report template for clients: what to include and what to leave out

A monthly report is not a copy of data from tools, but an explained selection. Its role is to answer a single question: what changed this month, and why?

The structure below works both for a client familiar with technical terms and for one who has never heard of crawl budget. Each section has a clear role and can be shortened or expanded according to the size of the contract.

Why a well-prepared monthly SEO report matters

SEO is an activity whose results are difficult to see from one month to the next. Without a clear report, the client sees only a monthly invoice and no visible connection to what they received in return, and the relationship weakens even if the work behind it is sound.

A good report prevents exactly this scenario. It connects the month's activities (articles published, technical fixes, links acquired) to their concrete effects: traffic, rankings, enquiries received through the form.

The report also has an internal role, often overlooked: it forces the team to check its own work before presenting it. A report that cannot be filled with real data signals a month without progress, and this must be acknowledged, not hidden behind vague wording.

There is also a direct commercial benefit. Clients who receive a clear monthly report renegotiate their contracts less often and rarely ask for further explanations by phone, because the information they would request is already in the document. Agencies that skip this step lose time to repeated questions that a well-planned report would have prevented from the first month.

What the report includes, section by section

A useful monthly report has four fixed blocks. The order matters: it begins with the result visible to the client (traffic) and ends with technical details, which most clients skim quickly.

Organic traffic and its trend

The first section shows the trend in visits from organic search, compared with the previous month and, if the history allows, with the same month last year. The data comes directly from Google Analytics 4, segmented by channel so the figures do not include visits from ads or social media.

Rankings for priority keywords

Report only the keywords agreed at the start of the work together, not every query in Search Console. Ten to fifteen phrases, with this month's ranking next to last month's, are enough to show the trend without overwhelming the reader.

Conversions and goals achieved

Traffic without conversions tells a business owner nothing. This section links organic visits to form enquiries, calls or sales, depending on the goal set for the website. If goals are not configured correctly, the month is lost to estimates, so check their configuration before the first report, not in the third month.

Technical problems fixed that month

The last block lists what was fixed: crawl errors, pages blocked by mistake, loading speed, invalid structured data. A regular technical SEO audit provides exactly this kind of list, ready to copy into the report, showing the difference between what was wrong and what was corrected.

Content published and links acquired

A short line about what was published on the blog and how many new links the website received from external sources completes the picture. There is no point detailing every article; the title, target keyword and, where appropriate, a direct link to the published page are enough. For incoming links, the source and its relevance matter, not just the raw count: five links from websites in the client's field say more than fifty from generic directories.

What to leave out of the monthly report

The exclusion list is as important as the content list. A report loaded with data unrelated to the client's goal tires the reader and hides precisely the part that matters.

  • The raw number of keywords for which the website appears somewhere in the top one hundred results, with no connection to search intent.
  • Screenshots of charts from third-party tools, without any explanation underneath of what the variation means.
  • Unexplained jargon: crawl budget, canonical, hreflang, without a sentence briefly explaining the term on its first appearance.
  • Comparisons with unnamed competitors or competitor figures you cannot verify publicly.
  • Promises about the position the website will hold next month. SEO does not guarantee a specific ranking.

The short rule for any line in the report: if you cannot explain aloud, in one sentence, why it is there, remove it.

Completed monthly report template, with hypothetical data

The example below uses hypothetical figures for a fictional online stationery shop. The structure stays identical regardless of the real client's field; only the figures and keywords change.

  • Organic traffic: 1 240 visits, compared with 1 080 last month, growth in the product category relaunched two months ago.
  • Rankings: "personalised stationery" rose from position 9 to position 5; the other priority keywords remained stable.
  • Conversions: 34 quote requests through the form, compared with 27 last month, all from organic traffic directly to category pages.
  • Technical: 12 product pages returning a 404 error were redirected correctly, and mobile loading time fell by 0,4 seconds.
  • Plan for next month: two new blog articles targeting "how to choose" intent, plus correcting structured data in the accessories category.

Every line in the example above follows the rule from the previous section: it can be explained on the spot, without additional notes.

How to present the report to the client

Sending the report by email without any discussion is the most common mistake. Good figures go unnoticed, while weak ones are misinterpreted without context.

A short call of ten to fifteen minutes, going through the report section by section, prevents both problems. The client can ask questions on the spot, and the agency can explain why a weaker figure is not a cause for concern, if it genuinely is not.

Another common mistake is a hasty promise. When a figure looks good, the temptation to promise the same growth next month is strong, but SEO does not work linearly. A good month can be followed by a stable one without that indicating a problem, and the report should leave room for this variation, not hide it behind forecasts no one can guarantee.

The discussion works better when the report already has a fixed structure agreed in the brief. A clear SEO brief at the start of the work together reduces misunderstandings about what the monthly report tracks and which goals were agreed with the client.

Which tools help you gather the data

Report data comes from a few fixed sources, not manually from dozens of different screens every month.

  • Google Search Console, for rankings, clicks and coverage reports, which show which pages are indexed and which have been excluded.
  • the Search Console setup guide, useful if the property was not fully connected at the start of the work together.
  • Google Analytics 4, for traffic by channel and conversions, with goals explicitly defined for each individual website.
  • Our own GOAI site analyzertool, useful for quickly checking technical problems that arose that month before they reach the report.

With these four sources connected correctly, preparing the report takes less than an hour per month, even for a portfolio of dozens of clients. Automating data exports by connecting Search Console and Analytics to a single automatically updated document also removes the risk of copying errors between screens, an easy mistake to make at the end of a busy month.

How often to send the report and who receives it

A monthly cadence works for most contracts, but it is not the only suitable option. A new website with less than three months of history has large month-to-month variations, and a monthly report can show declines that mean nothing in the long term.

  • Contracts in their first three months: monthly report, but focused on activities completed rather than figures, which are only starting to stabilise.
  • Mature contracts, with more than six months of history: full monthly report, with all four blocks described above.
  • Clients with large budgets and complex websites: alongside the monthly report, a quarterly summary comparing the longer-term trend.

The recipient matters as much as the cadence. If the report goes to someone in marketing, it can retain more technical terms with brief explanations. If it goes directly to the business owner, the conversions section and short closing conclusion must be readable on their own, without the rest of the document.

A good monthly SEO report is not a document for appearances, but the tool through which clients understand exactly what they bought. If you work with an agency or are considering starting this process internally, SEO optimisation supported by clear reports shows over time in results, not just invoices. For specific budgets and packages, the SEO optimisation pricing page shows what is included at each level of working together.
